title: Fourteen Years Later, Saif Ali Khan Finally Says It: Agent Vinod "Might Have Been Vain."
excerpt: In a rare unguarded reflection, the actor calls his ambitious 2012 spy thriller a film "ahead of its time" — and admits the dream project he produced for himself had too many toppings on the pizza.
body:
Some films never quite leave the people who made them. Fourteen years after Agent Vinod opened to a roar and faded to a whisper, Saif Ali Khan is still turning it over in his hands — and for once, he isn't defending it. He's diagnosing it.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=kWaWQCH48Sg

Speaking to Variety India, the actor did the thing stars almost never do about their expensive failures: he owned it, with a candour that's both disarming and a little wistful. "I think of Agent Vinod as a film that might have been vain," Saif said. "But also, that film opened really well, you know. It's just that it did not sustain because it probably wasn't a tightly made film, or it went off track in many ways."

**"Maybe we made some mistakes." — Saif Ali Khan

The most quietly devastating line in his reflection isn't his own — it's a confession he borrows from his director."**

That's a remarkable sentence from a man who produced the project as a personal passion. Agent Vinod was supposed to be his Bond — a globe-hopping, gadget-light spy thriller directed by Sriram Raghavan, the cult genius behind Ek Hasina Thi and, later, Andhadhun. It paired Saif with Kareena Kapoor Khan, one of the few times the real-life couple shared the screen. It opened strong. And then it simply... unravelled.

"Imagine a kind of spy movie ahead of its time, perhaps. It was a cool film, but it should have held more. Maybe we made some mistakes." — Saif Ali Khan

The most quietly devastating line in his reflection isn't his own — it's a confession he borrows from his director. "As Sriram himself said, he put too many toppings on the pizza," Saif recalled. "But the idea wasn't bad, and the title wasn't bad, and it was the right film to make." Anyone who has watched Agent Vinod knows exactly what that means: a film bursting with continents, conspiracies, KGB ghosts and nuclear suitcases, a movie so stuffed with ambition it forgot to breathe. Raghavan would go on to make the leaner, deadlier Andhadhun and become one of India's most revered storytellers. Agent Vinod, in hindsight, reads like the brilliant misfire he had to make first.

What's fascinating is how Saif refuses to let "vanity" become the whole story. He cops to the ambition — gleefully, even — but pushes back on the idea that ego sank the ship. "It was vanity. I was excited to do that. I made the film for myself, but it did open well. So its failure was not because it was a vain idea," he argued. It's a subtle, almost lawyerly distinction: yes, I made it to thrill myself; no, that's not why it died. The film died because it lost its shape.

His timing is no accident. The reflection arrives just weeks after Lalit Parimoo, a member of the Agent Vinod cast, lit a small fire on Siddharth Kannan's podcast by claiming the film failed because of "too much interference" from its star couple. "The way Sriram wanted to make that film, he couldn't make it that way," Parimoo alleged, arguing the writing and direction teams never got to fully realise their vision. Against that pointed accusation, Saif's own mea culpa lands differently — less a rebuttal than a quieter, more honest version of the same autopsy. He doesn't name the interference. He just admits the film went off track, and lets the reader fill in the rest.

For the diaspora, Agent Vinod occupies a strange, fond place in the memory. It was one of the early swings at a genuinely global Indian spy film — years before the YRF Spy Universe turned that idea into a billion-rupee machine with Tiger, War and the upcoming Alpha. Watched today, available on streaming platforms including Prime Video and JioHotstar in various markets, it plays almost like a prototype: too early, too crammed, but unmistakably reaching for something the industry would only learn to do well a decade later. "Ahead of its time" is the kind of thing every flop director says. In Agent Vinod's case, the spy-universe boom that followed makes it almost defensible.

There's a reason this kind of reflection resonates. Saif, now decades into a career that swung from Parampara to Omkara to Sacred Games, has earned the right to look back without flinching. He has nothing left to prove and no opening weekend to protect. So he tells the truth: it was vain, it was cool, it had a great title, and it should have held more.

The sharpest part of all this? Raghavan once said he and Saif should have made their Dr. No — a tight, realistic first film — instead of leaping straight to the franchise excess of an Octopussy. A sequel has been floated for years and never built. Maybe that's for the best. Some films are better as the beautiful mistake that taught everyone how to do it right next time. Agent Vinod, it turns out, was the rehearsal Indian cinema didn't know it was running.
